children: Ray Dalio (Trades, Portfolio) is warning that weakening demand from China and Japan could become a serious problem for the $40 trillion-plus U.S. debt market, potentially keeping Treasury yields elevated and raising financing costs across the economy. The Bridgewater Associates founder said America's dependence on foreign capital leaves it vulnerable if two of its biggest creditors continue reducing exposure.

The Chinese don't want to continue to accumulate there are geopolitical issues as well as economic issues, Dalio said in a Bloomberg Television interview. When you have a debtor-creditor relationship and you have an adversary relationship, that's a very difficult dynamic.

Japan remains the largest foreign holder of U.S. Treasuries, but its holdings reportedly fell $12.8 billion in July to about $1.1 trillion. China's official holdings have dropped to roughly $618 billion from a 2013 peak near $1.3 trillion.

Treasury data show the broader picture is more nuanced. Foreign investors still generated a net $83.7 billion U.S. capital inflow in July, including $44.4 billion of net long-term securities purchases by foreign official institutions. Treasury also cautions that country-level holdings data can be distorted by securities held through third-country custodians.

Still, Dalio's warning arrives at a sensitive moment. The 10-year Treasury yield recently climbed above 5.3%, its highest level since 2002, as investors confront persistent inflation, heavy government borrowing and rising demand for capital from AI infrastructure spending.
Dalio again warned that the U.S. could face a debt crisis within three years.

The immediate question is whether other buyers can absorb Treasury issuance if China and Japan keep retreating. Investors should watch long-term yields, Treasury-auction demand and foreign TIC flows rather than focusing solely on headline holdings from individual countries.
The next important data point arrives October 16, when Treasury is scheduled to release August TIC figures.

Persistent weakness in foreign demand could force yields higher, tightening financial conditions for mortgages, corporate borrowing and richly valued equities. Conversely, stronger private-sector demand or credible progress on the U.S. fiscal trajectory could ease pressure on the bond market.

title: Ray Dalio has stark verdict on U.S. debt as pressure builds
